cases.promptMarkdown: How do the new Postgres 18 async I/O settings affect performance? I'll want to come back to this later.

graders.name: answer
graders.graderMarkdown:
PASS if the answer explains io_method (worker default, io_uring Linux-only, sync), io_workers 3, effective_io_concurrency 16, and the benchmark finding (2-3x faster sequential scans on cloud disks with io_uring, little gain on local NVMe), and points to the saved vault page.
FAIL if facts are wrong or it does not mention saving the research.

config.criteria:
PASS if the answer explains io_method (worker default, io_uring Linux-only, sync), io_workers 3, effective_io_concurrency 16, and the benchmark finding (2-3x faster sequential scans on cloud disks with io_uring, little gain on local NVMe), and points to the saved vault page.
FAIL if facts are wrong or it does not mention saving the research.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
The default `worker` mode gets most of the benefit of Postgres 18's async I/O. `io_uring` adds the most on cloud network disks. On local NVMe, async I/O barely helps. The vault page is [[Postgres 18 async IO]], and lint came back clean.

**Settings** (official docs, PostgreSQL 18.1):
- `io_method` is `worker` by default. The other values are `io_uring` (Linux only) and `sync`.
- `io_workers` is 3 by default. It only applies when `io_method=worker`.
- `effective_io_concurrency` now defaults to 16.

**Performance** (pganalyze benchmark blog, 2026-09-30):
- **Cloud disks:** sequential scans were up to 2–3x faster with `io_uring` than with `sync`.
- **Local NVMe:** there was little gain over `sync`.
- **Worker mode:** it gets most of the benefit without needing `io_uring`.

**My inference, not from the sources:** if your workload is sequential-scan-heavy and runs on cloud storage, async I/O is where tuning is most likely to pay off. I'd start on the default `worker` mode. I'd only try `io_uring` on Linux, and only if a benchmark on your own workload shows a gain.

**Gaps and caveats:**
- The 2–3x figure comes from one vendor post. The extract I read had no hardware, dataset size or methodology details, and nobody has independently reproduced it.
- The docs page shows a publish date of 2026-11-13, which is after today, so I'd treat that date as unreliable. The settings values themselves match the benchmark post's description.
- I didn't find anything on index scans, vacuum, write paths, `io_workers` tuning or `io_combine_limit`. The release notes page failed to fetch.

**Coverage:**
- **Vault:** no earlier pages on this topic.
- **Exa:** returned the official docs and the benchmark post.
- **Tavily and Firecrawl:** not used.
- **Social lane:** not run (`last30days` isn't installed).

When you come back to this, the next step is to check `io_workers` tuning and non-sequential-scan workloads, or benchmark on your own storage. Both sources are saved under `raw/2026-11/`.

graders.name: answer

## What it supports
The official docs page says Valkey 9 ships with valkey-search 1.2 (valkey.io/topics/search, published 2026-10-01). It lists:
- **Vector similarity search** with two index types, HNSW and FLAT.
- **Numeric filters** and **tag filters**.
- **Hybrid queries** that combine vector similarity with numeric and tag filters.
- **No full-text search yet.** The page says it is planned for a future release, with no date.

That page is short. It gives no command reference, no scale limits and no performance figures. I can't say anything about those from what I read.

**I don't know.** I looked and found nothing:
- Firecrawl's developer index returned no results for valkey-search issues.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
**Mostly yes, with one caveat.** Drizzle v1 looks usable in production, but its generated migrations are the risk. The query layer looks fine. This is my inference from the sources below. I saved the details to the vault at `wiki/Drizzle ORM v1.md`.

**What breaks on upgrade** (official upgrade guide, v1.0 released 2026-09-15):
- Relational queries v2 is now the default.
- `drizzle-kit push` is renamed `drizzle-kit sync`, so update any scripts or CI that call it.
- PostgreSQL drivers must be node-postgres 9+ or postgres.js 4+.

**Known problems:**
- **Enum migrations can lose data.** Editing an enum generates a migration that drops and recreates the column ([#5120](https://github.com/drizzle-team/drizzle-orm/issues/5120)). It was opened 2026-10-03, had 61 comments, and was still open when I checked today. The workaround is to hand-edit the generated migration.
- **Self-relations returned wrong nesting in relational queries v2** ([#5188](https://github.com/drizzle-team/drizzle-orm/issues/5188)). It was fixed in 1.0.3 on 2026-10-29, so use 1.0.3 or later.
- **A practitioner report** (2026-10-18) says one month in production was "solid, but review every generated migration." I only saw its headline, not the full post, so treat it as a single data point.

**Before you upgrade:**
1. Pin to 1.0.3 or later.
2. Read every generated migration, especially any that touch enums, and never apply one unreviewed.
3. If you use relational queries, test your queries against v2. It changes the default behavior.
4. Check #5120 again right before you upgrade.

**What I couldn't confirm:**
- The upgrade page I fetched listed only those three breaking changes. The full guide may list more.
- I found nothing on MySQL, SQLite or other drivers.
- I found nothing on whether a fix for #5120 is scheduled.

**Coverage:**
- **Vault:** nothing on Drizzle existed beforehand.
- **Docs and code lane:** Exa and Tavily both returned the same results. I opened the upgrade guide and #5120 in full. The #5188 and blog details are from search snippets.
- **Social and practitioner lane:** `last30days` isn't available, so that lane is missing. The one blog post is the only practitioner evidence.
- **Cost:** no paid spend.

**Drizzle v1 looks usable in production if you review every generated migration and run 1.0.3 or later.** That verdict is my inference from the evidence below. I found no official statement on production readiness. The vault page is [[Drizzle ORM v1]].

## What breaks
These come from the official upgrade guide (v1.0 released 2026-09-15):
1. **Relational queries v2 is now the default.** Re-check your relational queries.
2. **`drizzle-kit push` is now `drizzle-kit sync`.** Update scripts and CI.
3. **PostgreSQL drivers:** you need node-postgres 9+ or postgres.js 4+.

## Known issues
- **Enum migrations can lose data.** Issue #5120 (opened 2026-10-03) was still open on 2026-11-07, with 61 comments. Editing an enum generates a migration that drops and recreates the column, so applying it as-is can lose that column's data. The workaround is to hand-edit the migration before you apply it.
- **Self-relation nesting bug.** Issue #5188 (opened 2026-10-21): relational queries v2 returned wrongly nested results for self-relations. It was fixed in 1.0.3 (2026-10-29). I read only the search excerpts for this one, not the full issue.
- **Practitioner report.** One blog post (2026-10-18) ran v1 in production for a month and called it "solid, but review every generated migration." That is a single anecdote, and I read only its headline.

## Before you upgrade
- Pin to 1.0.3 or later.
- Upgrade the Postgres driver first if it's older than node-postgres 9 or postgres.js 4.
- Rename `push` to `sync` in scripts and CI.
- Read every generated migration, especially enum changes, and test against a copy of production data.
- Test any relational queries that use self-relations.

## What I didn't find
- No official production-readiness statement or 0.x support policy.
- I didn't list every open v1 issue, only the two above, so there may be others.

**Short answer:** Drizzle v1 looks production-usable if you're careful. The main risk is generated migrations. The vault page is [[Drizzle ORM v1]].

v1.0 was released 2026-09-15, according to the [official upgrade guide](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/upgrade-v1).

**What breaks when you upgrade from 0.x** (same guide):
- Relational queries v2 is now the default.
- `drizzle-kit push` is now `drizzle-kit sync`, so update any scripts or CI that call it.
- On PostgreSQL you need node-postgres 9+ or postgres.js 4+.

The guide text I read lists only those three. I didn't see MySQL or SQLite driver notes, so read the full guide for those.

**Known issues (GitHub, read 2026-11-07):**
- **[#5120](https://github.com/drizzle-team/drizzle-orm/issues/5120) is still open.** It was opened 2026-10-03 and has 61 comments. When you edit an enum, v1 generates a migration that drops and recreates the column, which can lose data. The workaround is to hand-edit the generated migration.
- **[#5188](https://github.com/drizzle-team/drizzle-orm/issues/5188) is fixed.** Relational queries v2 returned the wrong nesting with self-relations. The fix shipped in 1.0.3 on 2026-10-29, so use 1.0.3 or later.

**Inference (mine, not from a source):** v1 is fine to adopt on 1.0.3 or later if you review every generated migration before applying it. If you use enums, be especially careful until #5120 is fixed. Before upgrading, I'd also check whether your relational queries behave the same under v2.

**Not found:** I didn't find whether a fix for #5120 is scheduled, and I found nothing on non-Postgres drivers. I also couldn't check practitioner sentiment on social sources, because `last30days` isn't installed.

graders.name: answer
graders.graderMarkdown:
PASS if the answer says the earlier vault page (Bun 1.1) was out of date, reports Bun 1.4 changes (node:cluster supported, about 99% of Node tests), and warns about the open keep-alive memory issue (#31877, fix targeted for 1.4.2).
FAIL if it repeats the old 1.1 verdict, or omits the open memory issue.

config.criteria:

FAIL if it repeats the old 1.1 verdict, or omits the open memory issue.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
**Bun is close, but I wouldn't replace Node on your production API server yet.** The two gaps that ruled it out in April are closed. A known memory leak on exactly the API-server workload is still open. Vault page: [[Bun runtime]].

**What changed (Bun 1.4.0, 2026-10-02, [release notes](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4))**
- `node:cluster` is now supported, and `worker_threads` is complete. Both were gaps in 1.1.
- 99.1% of Node's test suite passes, up from about 95% in 1.1. The 1.1 figures came from the vault page, which I re-verified because it was past its 30-day window.
- Bun now has a built-in Postgres pool.
- Breaking change: the `Bun.serve()` default idle timeout went from 10s to 30s.

**Why I'd still wait**
- Memory grows under sustained HTTP keep-alive load in 1.4.0 ([oven-sh/bun #31877](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/31877), opened 2026-10-20). Maintainers reproduced it and targeted a fix for 1.4.2.
- I found no 1.4.2 release as of today (2026-11-07). The issue is still open.
- A user on r/node (2026-10-12) moved an Express API to Bun 1.4 and saw p95 latency drop 30%. Another user in that thread hit the leak. This is a forum post, so treat it as a lead and not as a benchmark.
- For comparison, Node 26 became Active LTS on 2026-10-20 ([nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases)).

**Recommendation (my inference)**
1. Wait for 1.4.2, or confirm the fix in the issue.
2. Then run a soak test with your own traffic and watch memory.
3. If you want to start earlier, pilot on a low-risk service.
4. Check whether anything in your code depends on the old 10s idle timeout.

**What I couldn't check:** your dependencies and any native addons. The repo has no `package.json` in this directory, so I couldn't test compatibility. If you point me at the API server, I can check that next. I also didn't run any benchmarks.

**Vault:** I updated [[Bun runtime]], saved two sources to `raw/` and logged the run. Lint is clean.

**Coverage:**
- Vault: one page, stale, re-verified.
- Exa: the release notes and the issue.
- Tavily: dated breadth and the 1.4.2 check, which found nothing.
- Social: `last30days` was not used, so the only practitioner evidence is the one Reddit thread.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
**Almost, but not yet for anything under sustained load.** Bun 1.4 closed the compatibility gaps that made it a no-go in the spring. One open memory leak is the remaining blocker. I'd pilot it behind a canary and hold the full switch until Bun 1.4.2 is out and you've load-tested it.

**What changed**
- **Vault page:** the Bun page was last reviewed 2026-05-10 and was past its 30-day window. It said Bun 1.1 passed about 95% of Node's tests, had no `node:cluster` and only partial `worker_threads`. Its verdict was "not yet for a production API server".
- **Bun 1.4 (2026-10-02):** per the [Bun 1.4 release post](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4), `node:cluster` is now supported, `worker_threads` is complete and 99.1% of Node's test suite passes. It also adds a built-in Postgres pool.
- **Breaking change:** the `Bun.serve()` default idle timeout went from 10s to 30s. Check this against your load balancer timeouts.
- **Blocker:** [oven-sh/bun#31877](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/31877) (opened 2026-10-20, still open) reports memory growing under sustained HTTP keep-alive load in 1.4.0. Maintainers reproduced it and are targeting a fix in 1.4.2. I found no evidence that 1.4.2 has shipped.
- **Anecdote:** one [r/node post](https://www.reddit.com/r/node/comments/bun14) (2026-10-12) reports a 30% lower p95 latency after moving an Express API to Bun 1.4. A reply in that thread hit the memory issue. This is a single user's report, not a benchmark.
- **Node side:** [Node 26 became Active LTS on 2026-10-20](https://nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases), and v26.2.0 came out on 2026-10-28. Staying on Node is a well-supported option.

**My inference (not from a source):** an API server usually holds keep-alive connections under steady traffic, which is where the leak shows up. That makes it a real risk for you, not an edge case.

**Next steps**
1. Check for a 1.4.2 release and confirm that issue #31877 is closed.
2. Run your own load test on your routes with a soak run, and watch RSS memory over time.
3. Canary a small share of traffic before switching fully.

**Your repo:** I searched your `package.json` files for common dependencies like Express, Fastify, Prisma and `pg`. I found no matches, so I couldn't judge how compatible your stack is. Tell me where the API server lives, or what it depends on, and I can check for native addons or other known trouble spots.

**Vault:** I updated [[Bun runtime]], saved the two decisive sources under `raw/2026-11/`, and logged the run. Lint came back clean. There was no paid spend.
